CausalChain: Increased dietary linoleic acid -> Elevated circulating linoleic acid -> Upregulation of CPT1 in liver immune cells -> Enhanced fatty acid oxidation in CD4⁺ T cells -> Apoptosis of CD4⁺ T cells -> Reduced tumor immunosurveillance -> Promotion of HCC progression
Hypothesis: Elevated levels of dietary and circulating linoleic acid in NAFLD patients induce CPT1 expression in CD4⁺ T lymphocytes, leading to their accelerated apoptosis and impaired tumor immune surveillance, thereby promoting hepatocarcinogenesis. Therapeutic modulation of CPT1 activity or dietary fatty acid composition could restore immune function and mitigate HCC progression.
Abstract: This study proposes a novel hypothesis linking aberrant free fatty acid (FFA) signaling to impaired immunosurveillance in the progression of non‐alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) to hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). We hypothesize that elevated dietary and circulating levels of specific n‐6 polyunsaturated fatty acids such as linoleic acid lead to upregulation of key metabolic enzymes, including carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1 (CPT1), in the hepatic milieu. Enhanced CPT1 activity then accelerates fatty acid oxidation in CD4⁺ T lymphocytes, triggering their apoptosis and thereby diminishing antitumor immunity. This metabolic reprogramming may foster an immunosuppressive microenvironment that facilitates tumor growth. The interplay between dietary fatty acids, immune cell metabolic shifts, and oncogenic liver pathways therefore offers a new target for therapeutic intervention.
